idiom_name: two-index compaction loop + explicit length update (memmove for range gaps)
implementation_notes: C has no generic algorithms and no container type that owns a length, so the idiom is the loop itself: scan with a read cursor and copy each retained element down to a write cursor (a[w++] = a[r]), then perform the release step by hand - assign the new length and zero or clear the dead tail. When a contiguous range has to go rather than a predicate's worth of elements, memmove closes the gap in one call because it is specified to handle overlapping objects, which is the closest thing C has to a batch erase. What replaces the classic structure: nothing - both halves are hand-written and their correctness (length bookkeeping, tail release, overlap-safe copies) is the programmer's responsibility, which is why languages that own the length absorbed this into a member function. Keep the loop when the array is a struct member with a separate count or when the memory layout is the point.
pitfalls: Storage and length are separate: forgetting to update n (or the count field that carries it) leaves the removed elements live and lets later reads run past the intended end.

Manual compaction leaves copies of the removed elements in the tail - for pointer arrays that is a double free or use after free waiting to happen, and for secrets it is data remanence. Zero or overwrite the dead tail.
memmove, not memcpy, whenever source and destination overlap; memcpy's behaviour is undefined for overlapping ranges.
Element count versus byte count: the copy step must move whole elements (or sizeof *a bytes each), and the destination must have room for the survivors in place.
sources: cppreference, memmove, memmove_s - copies count characters between objects that may overlap, 'as if the characters were copied to a temporary character array and then ... copied from the array to dest': https://en.cppreference.com/w/c/string/byte/memmove
